claims.text: A drainage basin is all the land whose rainfall drains into one river and the streams that join it; the watershed is the high land that separates one drainage basin from another, a tributary is a smaller river that joins a larger one, and the confluence is the point where two rivers join.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Rain reaching a drainage basin takes several paths: some is intercepted by leaves, some soaks into the soil by infiltration, some moves through the soil towards the river as throughflow, some sinks to rock as groundwater flow, some evaporates, and what cannot soak in runs over the surface as overland flow; the more water that soaks in, the slower and lower the river's response to a storm, so a well-vegetated, absorbent basin feeds its river gently while a bare or paved basin sends a fast, high flood peak downstream.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A river's characteristics change along its course: downstream the channel typically becomes wider and deeper, its speed first falls over rough beds and then may rise again as the channel smooths, and its discharge, the volume of water passing a point each second, grows steadily as tributaries join, so a river near its mouth is usually far larger than near its source.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Rivers flow from their source, where the channel begins, downhill to their mouth, where the river ends at the sea or a lake; a tributary joins the main river, whereas a distributary splits away from it as in a delta, so reading a map backwards, or calling a joining channel a distributary, swaps the river's whole direction.

claims.text: The causes of a flood - heavy rainfall, melting snow, deforestation that cuts interception, and urban surfaces that seal the soil - all act before the flood; the impacts - drowned crops, ruined homes, people made homeless - all come after it, so a question about causes is not answered by listing impacts.

claims.text: A river erodes by hydraulic action, the force of water and air compressed into cracks breaking the bed and banks; by abrasion, the load of stones and sand the water carries being thrown against the bed and banks to grind them; and by corrosion, water dissolving soluble rock such as limestone.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A river transports its load dissolved in solution, suspended in the water, or bounced and dragged along the bed; the faster the flow, the larger the particles it can move, so when the current slows - entering a lake, a sea or a gentle stretch - the river drops its load, heaviest particles first, which is deposition.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: On a meander bend the water flows fastest on the outside and slowest on the inside, so erosion carves a river cliff on the outer bend while deposition builds a slip-off slope on the inner bend; an oxbow lake forms when the neck between two bends is cut through in a flood and deposition then seals the cut-off, and a delta too is built by deposition where a river slows and drops its load at its mouth.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A river's long profile falls steeply from source towards mouth, and its valley changes shape along the way: in the upper course vertical erosion cuts a steep-sided gorge, over a band of resistant rock differential erosion leaves a waterfall whose plunge pool undercuts the hard lip until it collapses and the fall retreats upstream, and potholes are worn where stones grind the rocky bed in eddies.

claims.text: In the middle and lower course a river spreads over a wide, flat flood plain - flat land beside a river covered by water when it floods - and loops in meanders; in floods the river spreads over its banks, drops coarse sediment along the channel edge to build raised levées, and lays finer silt across the plain, while at the mouth slow, checked water and deposition at the sea build a delta crossed by distributaries.

claims.text: A landform question first asks what the feature is like - its shape, size with a scale and position - and only a question with Explain asks how it formed; describing the formation when the command word asks for the features is the wrong angle for the question asked.

claims.text: Rivers flood when more water reaches the channel than it can carry - after heavy or prolonged rainfall, when snow melts rapidly, where deforestation has cut interception and infiltration, and where towns' roofs and roads send rain straight to the channel as overland flow - and flooding may also erode banks and undermine buildings beside the channel.

claims.text: Flooding brings hazards: crops drown and topsoil is stripped, homes and their contents are ruined, people drown or are made homeless, and disease spreads in stagnant water and spoiled supplies.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Rivers and their flood plains offer opportunities: flat, easy land to build and farm on, fertile silt renewed by each flood, water for irrigation, homes and industry, fish to catch, and cheap, gentle transport along the valley, which is why people have always settled beside rivers even where they flood.

claims.text: River flooding can be managed by engineering works - dams and reservoirs that store floodwater, raised embankment walls that contain the channel, and channel straightening and deepening that speed water away - and by softer measures: flood-plain zoning that steers building off the lowest ground, afforestation that increases infiltration across the basin, and flood warnings that give people time to move.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Each management choice carries costs and limits: dams and embankments are costly to build and protect where they stand, while zoning, afforestation and warnings cost little but change no flood on their own, so the better scheme depends on the place - the size of the settlement, the money available and how much warning the river gives.

claims.text: The Orange is southern Africa's longest river: it rises as the Senqu in the mountains of Lesotho, flows westward about 2,200 kilometres across South Africa, forms the border between South Africa and Namibia over its last stretch, and enters the Atlantic at Alexander Bay, plunging on the way through the Augrabies Falls, about 60 metres, in a rocky gorge.

claims.text: The Orange presents opportunities along its lower valley, where rainfall is often under 100 millimetres a year: irrigation schemes at Aussenkehr and Noordoewer on the Namibian stretch pump river water onto vineyards that grow table grapes for export, and upstream the Gariep Dam, completed in 1971 and South Africa's largest reservoir, stores water for towns and farms and generates hydro-electric power.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Orange's hazard is flooding in the summer rainy season: in 1988, one of the largest floods of the twentieth century on the river inundated camps and vineyards along the lower Orange, damaging the irrigation schemes around Kakamas and Aussenkehr and sweeping away pumps and piping.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Flooding on the lower Orange is managed rather than stopped: the Gariep Dam (1971) and the Vanderkloof Dam (1977) upstream store and release water steadily, which lowers the flood peaks reaching the irrigation schemes, and the schemes themselves are protected by embankment walls and rebuilt pump stations, though summer floods still interrupt farming, so the management has partly succeeded rather than solved the hazard.
